prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

O blithe New-comer! I have heard, I hear thee and rejoice. O Cuckoo! shall I call thee Bird, Or but a wandering Voice? While I am lying on the grass Thy twofold shout I hear; From hill to hill it seems to pass, At once far off, and near. Though babbling only to the Vale Of sunshine and of flowers, Thou bringest unto me a tale Of visionary hours. Thrice welcome, darling of the Spring! Even yet thou art to me No bird, but an invisible thing, A voice, a mystery; The same whom in my school-boy days I listened to; that Cry Which made me look a thousand ways In bush, and tree, and sky. To seek thee did I often rove Through woods and on the green; And thou wert still a hope, a love; Still longed for, never seen. And I can listen to thee yet; Can lie upon the plain And listen, till I do beget That golden time again. O blessèd Bird! the earth we pace Again appears to be An unsubstantial, faery place; That is fit home for Thee!

outputs.L1:
O blithe newcomer! I have heard—  
I hear thee and rejoice.  
O Cuckoo! Shall I call thee bird,  
Or but a wandering voice?

While I am lying on the grass,  
Thy twofold shout I hear;  
From hill to hill it seems to pass,  
At once far off and near.

Though babbling only to the vale  
Of sunshine and of flowers,  
Thou bringest unto me a tale  
Of visionary hours.

Thrice welcome, darling of the spring!  
Even yet thou art to me  
No bird, but an invisible thing—  
A voice, a mystery;

The same whom, in my schoolboy days,  
I listened to—that cry  
Which made me look a thousand ways,  
In bush and tree and sky.

To seek thee did I often rove  
Through woods and on the green;  
And thou wert still a hope, a love—  
Still longed for, never seen.

And I can listen to thee yet;  
Can lie upon the plain  
And listen, till I do beget  
That golden time again.

O blessèd bird! The earth we pace  
Again appears to be  
An unsubstantial, faery place—  
A fitting home for thee!
outputs.L2:
Joyful herald newly come,  
I heard you then and hear you now with gladness.  
Cuckoo, should I think of you as a bird,  
Or merely as a roaming sound?

As I rest upon the grass,  
Your double call reaches me,  
Traveling as though from one hill to another,  
Seeming distant and close at the same moment.

Though your song is addressed only to a valley  
Bright with sunlight and filled with flowers,  
It carries me back to memories  
Of dreamlike hours.

Beloved sign of spring, you are welcome three times over!  
Even now, you seem to me  
Not a bird, but an unseen presence—  
A mysterious voice.

You are the same one I heard as a schoolboy,  
Whose cry sent my eyes searching everywhere:  
Among the bushes, through the trees,  
And across the sky.

I often wandered in pursuit of you,  
Crossing woods and open fields;  
Yet you always remained a hope and a cherished wonder,  
Forever desired but never seen.

Still, I can listen to you now  
While stretched upon the open ground,  
And continue hearing you until  
Those golden days return in my imagination.

Blessed bird, your call transforms the earth beneath our feet,  
Making it seem once more  
Like an insubstantial, enchanted realm—  
A fitting home for you.
outputs.L3:
The speaker is filled with joy when he hears the cuckoo’s distinctive call echoing across the hills. Although the bird itself remains hidden, its song seems to travel freely through the landscape. The cuckoo appears less like a physical creature than a mysterious, wandering voice—one that sounds distant at one moment and remarkably near the next.

Its call awakens vivid memories of the speaker’s childhood. As a boy, he searched eagerly for the unseen bird among woods, bushes, and trees, looking upward into the sky in the hope of catching sight of it. Yet the cuckoo always remained beyond his reach. Because it was heard but never seen, it gradually became more than an ordinary bird: it turned into an enduring symbol of hope, love, and longing.

Hearing the cuckoo again restores the speaker’s youthful sense of wonder. Its voice brings back the “golden” days of childhood, when the natural world seemed full of mystery and possibility. Under the spell of the bird’s call, the familiar earth is transformed into an enchanted, fairy-like place where imagination and reality meet.
outputs.L4:
In William Wordsworth’s “To the Cuckoo,” the speaker welcomes the bird as a joyful herald of spring. Although he hears its distinctive call echoing across hills and valleys, he cannot see where the sound comes from. This uncertainty makes the cuckoo seem less like an ordinary bird than a mysterious, wandering voice that belongs everywhere and nowhere at once. Its song fills the landscape, passing from one place to another and awakening the speaker’s imagination.

The call also carries him back to childhood, when he searched through woods, bushes, and open fields in the hope of finding the hidden bird. Even then, the cuckoo remained elusive, existing for him somewhere between reality and dream. Hearing it again restores that “golden time,” when the natural world seemed full of secrets and possibilities. Through the cuckoo’s voice, the familiar earth is transformed into an enchanted, almost fairy-like realm, preserving the childhood sense of wonder, mystery, and imaginative freedom.

At the first light of spring, a **new** sound echoed through the forest. High in an old oak tree, a **cuckoo** called across the quiet valley. The small **bird** had returned after a long journey, bringing with it the promise of warmer days. As its familiar song filled the air, the forest seemed to wake from its winter sleep.
